s: Columbia Sportswear DEF 14A filed 2026-04-24 (ownership as of 2026-04-06); COLM close 60.33 dollars on 2026-08-21
m: 3,183,963 COLM shares in the 2026 proxy x 60.33 dollars = 192M dollars; 181M dollars net of 178,376 unexercised options
did: Fourth-generation Boyle who joined Columbia Sportswear in 2005 as a merchandiser, ran Columbia-brand merchandising and design, and was named President of the Columbia brand in November 2025. He holds 3.18 million shares, 6.2 percent of the company, alongside his father Tim Boyle at 45.7 percent.
why: Columbia never sold control. The family kept a supermajority through the 1998 IPO and Tim Boyle moved blocks into grantor retained annuity trusts, so the stake passed down intact rather than being diluted by acquisition currency or broken up to pay estate tax.
obst: Rising inside a company his father runs meant every promotion drew nepotism scrutiny, and the 2026 proxy shows the governance committee ratifying his pay separately; he took the brand presidency in the year operating income fell 24 percent to 207 million dollars on tariffs.
turn: November 2025, when the board split the president role and handed him the Columbia brand, the unit that is most of group revenue, putting him in line to run the company.

s: SEC Forms 4, CIK 1236787, 2003-2014; Precision Castparts DEFM14A filed 2015-10-13, merger consideration and golden-parachute tables
m: 224.2M dollars of open-market Form 4 sales 2003-2014 plus 53.2M dollars of shares and 93.0M dollars of options, deferred comp and change-of-control pay at Berkshire's 235 dollar per share close, less roughly 30 percent tax
did: Ran Precision Castparts as CEO from 2002, buying Special Metals, Titanium Metals and Rolls-Royce parts plants until it was the qualified supplier of forged jet-engine discs, blades and airframe fasteners, then sold it to Berkshire Hathaway in January 2016 at 235 dollars a share, about 37 billion dollars.
why: Aerospace castings are qualified part by part by the FAA and the engine makers, so once a foundry is named on a GE or Boeing drawing, switching suppliers takes years. Donegan bought the qualified capacity instead of competing on price, then priced to the switching cost.
obst: The 2015-2016 oil and gas collapse gutted his energy segment and forced thousands of layoffs just as he was selling the company, and shareholders sued claiming 235 dollars a share undervalued the aerospace franchise.
turn: 25 July 2015, when he flew to Omaha and pushed Warren Buffett from an opening bid to a final 235 dollars a share in cash, cashing his options and deferred stock in one event.

s: SEC Forms 4, CIK 1170769, 2003-2024; Lithia Motors DEF 14A filed 2026-03-11 (age 82, 25,615 shares); LAD close 370.73 dollars on 2026-08-21
m: 141.3M dollars of Form 4 open-market LAD sales 2003-2024 less roughly 25 percent tax, plus 26,137 residual shares at 370.73 dollars
did: Took over his father's single Medford, Oregon Dodge store in 1968, listed Lithia Motors in December 1996 with about a dozen stores, and rolled it into a 300-plus-store group now selling 37.9 billion dollars of vehicles a year. He has sold 141 million dollars of Lithia stock since 2003.
why: Lithia bought rural and small-metro dealerships that the national chains ignored, at three to five times earnings, kept the selling family's sales staff, and plugged each store into one centralised finance and insurance desk. The margin came from the F and I attach rate, not the car.
obst: The 2008-2009 credit freeze nearly ended it: floorplan lenders pulled lines, Chrysler and GM cancelled franchises, and Lithia closed stores and cut its dividend while the shares fell below 3 dollars.
turn: December 1996, when he listed Lithia with a dual-class structure that let him keep voting control while issuing stock as acquisition currency.

s: SEC Form 4 dated 2026-01-09, CIK 1170767 (204,845 shares); Lithia Motors DEF 14A filed 2026-03-11 (age 59); LAD close 370.73 dollars on 2026-08-21
m: 204,845 LAD shares at 370.73 dollars = 75.9M dollars, plus 53.3M dollars of Form 4 sales 2004-2024 less roughly 25 percent tax
did: Joined his father's Lithia Motors in 1989, ran the acquisition machine through the 1996 IPO roll-up, and as CEO since 2012 took revenue from about 3 billion to 37.9 billion dollars while building Driveway, the online used-car channel, and buying Britain's Jardine and Pendragon networks.
why: The model is an arbitrage on private dealership multiples: pay three to five times earnings for a family store, refinance the real estate, and run it on shared inventory and finance systems. He industrialised the diligence so Lithia could close roughly a store a week.
obst: He launched Driveway straight into Carvana's 2020-2021 capital advantage, then had to defend the spend when the used-vehicle price bubble burst in 2022 and Lithia stock roughly halved.
turn: 2021, when Lithia bought Michigan's Suburban Collection and set a 50 billion dollar revenue target, turning a regional roll-up into a national one.

s: SEC Forms 4, CIK 937952, 2006-2022; Greenbrier DEF 14A filed 2021-11-10 (age 77); GBX close 46.05 dollars on 2026-08-21
m: 135.6M dollars of Form 4 open-market GBX sales 2006-2022 less roughly 25 percent tax, plus 672,518 shares last reported July 2021 at 46.05 dollars
did: Co-founded Greenbrier in 1981 as a railcar leasing shop in Lake Oswego, bought the Gunderson railcar plant on the Portland waterfront in 1985, and built North America's largest maker of intermodal and tank cars, with low-cost assembly at Monclova in Mexico. He was CEO until 2022.
why: Railcars are ordered in thousand-unit lots by leasing companies, so Greenbrier paired manufacturing with its own lease fleet and fleet-management arm and could take orders rivals could not finance. Building the cars in Mexico let it keep quoting through the down cycles.
obst: He fought off Carl Icahn's American Railcar, which took a stake and pushed a merger in 2008 and again in 2014-2015, then absorbed the collapse in crude-by-rail tank car orders after the post-Lac-Megantic tank car rules landed.
turn: 1985, when he bought the Gunderson plant out of Fruehauf and turned a leasing broker into a manufacturer.

s: SEC Forms 4, CIK 1237085, 2003-2019; NIKE FY2019 Form 10-K executive officer table (age 55 in July 2019); NKE close 40.76 dollars on 2026-08-21
m: 160.9M dollars of Form 4 open-market NIKE sales 2003-2019 less roughly 30 percent tax, plus 150,034 shares last reported December 2019 at 40.76 dollars
did: Joined NIKE in 1993 as a finance director, ran global footwear from 2001, and was chief operating officer from 2013 to 2020, owning the contract-factory base. He moved shoe assembly toward Vietnam and pushed Flyknit and automated cutting to strip labour content out of an upper.
why: NIKE owns no factories, so the leverage sits with whoever controls allocation across the contract manufacturers. Sprunk ran that allocation for two decades, and his option grants were struck against the 2005-2019 stretch when NIKE stock rose roughly tenfold.
obst: He was the executive who had to answer for Asian labour conditions after the sweatshop years, then hold the supply chain together through the 2011 Thai floods and the 2020 Vietnam plant shutdowns, and he was passed over for CEO before retiring in 2020.
turn: 2013, when Mark Parker made him chief operating officer with footwear manufacturing attached, converting a finance career into the equity grants that produced the money.

s: nLIGHT DEF 14A filed 2026-04-24 (age 61, 1,252,963 shares); SEC Forms 4, CIK 1738235, 2018-2026; LASR close 47.39 dollars on 2026-08-21
m: 1,252,963 LASR shares in the 2026 proxy at 47.39 dollars = 59.4M dollars, plus 63.2M dollars of Form 4 sales 2018-2026 less roughly 25 percent tax
did: Co-founded nLIGHT in 2000 to build semiconductor diode lasers in southwest Washington, took it public in 2018, and pivoted it from Chinese industrial cutting lasers into US directed-energy weapons. In 2026 nLIGHT won a 627 million dollar Joint Laser Weapon System award.
why: nLIGHT fabricates its own laser diodes rather than buying them, so when the Pentagon needed a domestic, export-clean high-energy laser source there were very few qualified vendors. The vertical integration that crushed margins in the commercial market became the moat in defence.
obst: Chinese fiber-laser makers gutted his industrial business after the 2018 IPO and the stock fell under 8 dollars; he funded the defence pivot out of a shrinking commercial base, and China export controls were still delaying commercial shipments in 2026.
turn: 2018, when US primes began sourcing directed-energy laser modules from nLIGHT, turning a commodity laser maker into a defence supplier.
